challenges.name: Cell Streak
challenges.note: Nine correct actions in a row

hazards.arm-envelope: You stepped inside the robot's reach envelope with the controller still in automatic. The arm does not know you are there and it does not slow down for you — the ring on this floor is set from the arm's own reach and stopping distance, calculated exactly the way ANSI/RIA R15.06 and its international counterpart ISO 10218 both require, not from how careful you feel walking up to it.
hazards.curtain-bypass: That jumper defeats the light curtain. The curtain is the only thing that stops the arm the instant a body crosses the plane — bypassing it to 'just check something quickly' is exactly how reach-in injuries happen.
hazards.pinch-point: That is the gripper's closing pinch point. Even in manual jog mode a six-axis end effector closes with enough force to crush a hand.
hazards.residual-air: That pneumatic line is still charged. Electrical lockout does not bleed stored air — a charged actuator can still fire the gripper with the power off.

interrupts.alert: The plant compressor has cut back in somewhere down the shop. The receiver gauge you bled to zero is reading four bar and still climbing.
interrupts.cue: You vented the air. Nothing isolated it.
interrupts.missNote: You opened the gate and reached into the end effector with the pneumatics back up. A charged actuator closes on a stuck pilot, a leaking solenoid or a knock on the valve body, and the electrics being dead does not enter into it — which is precisely why air carries a lockout of its own.
interrupts.why: Bleeding a receiver empties it; it does nothing to stop the shop main filling it again the moment demand comes back on the compressor. Electrical lockout covers one energy source and this cell has two, which is why a bleed valve on a lockout procedure is locked open rather than merely opened. You are two steps from putting a hand between the jaws of a gripper that now has six bar behind it and no controller involved in the decision.
interrupts.wrongNote: That is not where the stored energy is. The receiver is on the bleed valve, and it goes back to zero and stays there.

interrupts.alert: The cell gate has swung most of the way shut behind you. A few more degrees and the interlock latches with you standing inside the fence.
interrupts.cue: The open gate is the only thing telling this cell that somebody is in it.
interrupts.missNote: The gate latched while you had both hands in the end effector. Nothing came of it this time because your lock was on the disconnect, and that is the only reason — the cell went back to looking exactly like a cell that is clear, with a technician inside the envelope.
interrupts.why: An interlock is not a person-detector. It knows one thing — whether the gate is closed — and the reason you left it standing open is that a closed gate plus a reset at the HMI is a cell that believes it is empty. Your lock on the disconnect is the isolation; the open gate is the part of it that anybody walking up can read without going to look for a tag. So it gets chocked or held open, not left to a hinge and a draught.
interrupts.wrongNote: That is not what is closing on you. It is the gate, and it needs to be back open before your hands go near the arm again.

lateNotes.jammed-part: The gripper is only touched after the arm is proven at zero energy, air included.
lateNotes.teach-pendant: The pendant does not come off the hook until the cell is confirmed safe to jog.

name: Robot Cell

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Confirm the cell, the task and the isolation points listed.
steps.prompt: Confirm the cell, the task and the isolation points listed.
steps.title: Read the maintenance work order
steps.why: Cells share safety zones on some lines, and the isolation point for the arm next to yours does not necessarily cover the one you are about to open. Confirming the cell number and disconnect ID against the work order before you touch anything is what stops you locking out the wrong machine entirely.

steps.cue: Press the e-stop at the cell HMI before opening anything.
steps.prompt: Press the e-stop at the cell HMI before opening anything.
steps.title: Hit the cell emergency stop
steps.why: E-stop pulls the program out of automatic the instant you press it, but it is a control-level stop, not an energy isolation — the drive can still be reset from the HMI by someone who has no idea you are about to open the fence. Hitting it first buys you the seconds you need to isolate properly, nothing more.

steps.cue: Grab the cell's main power disconnect and rotate it to off.
steps.prompt: Grab the cell's main power disconnect and rotate it to off.
steps.title: Open the main disconnect
steps.why: The e-stop only halted the program; the disconnect is what actually removes the 480 V feed to the drives. OSHA's lockout/tagout rule at 29 CFR 1910.147 exists precisely because a cell that only e-stopped can be reset from the HMI by someone who has no idea a technician is standing inside the fence.

steps.cue: Apply your padlock to the disconnect hasp.
steps.prompt: Apply your padlock to the disconnect hasp.
steps.title: Lock the disconnect
steps.why: Your lock says the isolation belongs to you and nobody else. Whoever is chasing the line-down window will look for the fastest way back to production, and the only thing standing between that pressure and a re-energised cell with your hands still inside it is a padlock only you hold the key to.

steps.cue: Vent the air receiver and confirm the gauge reads zero.
steps.prompt: Vent the air receiver and confirm the gauge reads zero.
steps.title: Bleed the pneumatic system
steps.why: Stored compressed air moves an actuator with the electrics stone dead. Bleeding the receiver and isolating the shop main are two different problems, and this cell's gripper can still close on six bar of pressure with the main disconnect open and locked. Zero energy means every energy source, not just the one with a switch on it.

steps.cue: Meter the controller's drive input and commit when it reads dead.

gauge.label: DRIVE INPUT — VOLTAGE
gauge.missNote: Still reading live. Treat every check as if it might be hot, the way NFPA 70E expects, and recheck the disconnect and isolation point before the guard comes open.

steps.prompt: Meter the controller's drive input and commit when it reads dead.
steps.title: Verify zero energy at the controller
steps.why: An open disconnect is not proof by itself — a welded contactor, a miswired feed or a fault downstream can leave a path live behind a switch that reads open. You meter the drive input the same way for every isolation: watch the number, not the switch position, and commit only when it actually reads dead.

steps.cue: Open the interlocked gate now that the cell is proven dead.
steps.prompt: Open the interlocked gate now that the cell is proven dead.
steps.title: Open the cell gate
steps.why: The interlock exists specifically to stop this step from happening before isolation is proven — a closed gate plus a reset at the HMI is a cell that believes nobody is inside it. With the drive input confirmed dead at zero volts, opening the fence is finally the one moment it is actually safe to do.

steps.cue: Drag the jammed part free of the gripper jaws and into the return bin.

drag.missNote: Not clear of the jaws — carry it fully into the return bin, not back between the fingers.

steps.prompt: Drag the jammed part free of the gripper jaws and into the return bin.
steps.title: Service the end effector
steps.why: With the arm at zero energy and the receiver bled to nothing, the gripper has stopped being an energy source and become a mechanism you can put your hands into. Skip either isolation and it is still a six-axis end effector capable of closing with enough force to crush a hand.

steps.cue: Remove your lock and close the disconnect once you are clear of the envelope.
steps.prompt: Remove your lock and close the disconnect once you are clear of the envelope.
steps.title: Restore power and unlock
steps.why: Your lock, your call — removing it means confirming with your own eyes that every hand that was inside the envelope is now clear of it, because the moment the disconnect closes the cell believes it is fully staffed and ready to run in automatic again.

steps.cue: Jog the arm and keep speed inside the reduced-speed limit.

gauge.label: TEACH MODE — JOG SPEED
gauge.missNote: Over the teach-mode speed cap. That limit is what keeps a reflex reaction fast enough to matter.

steps.prompt: Jog the arm and keep speed inside the reduced-speed limit.
steps.title: Jog the arm in teach mode
steps.why: Teach mode caps jog speed well below production rate for one reason: a person is standing at the pendant with a dead-man switch, inside the envelope, instead of behind a fence. That speed cap is what keeps a reflex reaction fast enough to matter if something swings the wrong way.

steps.cue: Jog to each point and press teach, in the order the part actually travels.

itemNotes.wp-pick: Recorded right over the part in the infeed fixture.
itemNotes.wp-transfer: High enough to clear the fence rail on the way across the cell.

steps.outOfOrderNote: That point comes later in the part's actual path. Teach pick, then transfer, then place — playback runs the points in the order you recorded them, not the order that seems obvious.
steps.prompt: Jog to each point and press teach, in the order the part actually travels.
steps.title: Teach the pick-and-place waypoints
steps.why: A taught path is only as safe as the order it was recorded in. Teach the transfer waypoint after the place point and the controller plays them back in recording order, not travel order — the arm swings back through the fence line on its way to a position it should already have cleared.

steps.cue: Commit the three points to the controller as one program.
steps.prompt: Commit the three points to the controller as one program.
steps.title: Save the taught program
steps.why: An untaught point list is jog history sitting in the pendant's memory, not a program. Saving it is the step that turns three recorded positions into something the controller can actually execute unattended — skip it and the next run cycle has nothing to play back.

steps.cue: Hold RUN/VERIFY and watch the whole path clear the fence and the fixtures.
steps.holdBreakNote: Released before the dry-run finished. Hold it through the entire path — that's the only way to catch a bad point before it runs in production.
steps.prompt: Hold RUN/VERIFY and watch the whole path clear the fence and the fixtures.
steps.title: Dry-run the program at teach speed
steps.why: You verify a brand-new program at teach speed with your own hand on the pendant's dead-man switch, watching every point clear the fence and the fixtures, because the alternative is finding a bad waypoint the first time the cell runs it at full production speed with the guard closed and nobody watching.

steps.cue: Close the gate and confirm the interlock re-engages.
steps.prompt: Close the gate and confirm the interlock re-engages.
steps.title: Close and verify the guard
steps.why: A gate that swings shut without re-engaging its interlock will run the cell in automatic with the guard mechanically closed and electrically still open — the controller reports a closed gate, not a working interlock, so you confirm the re-engagement itself, not just the position.
